summary: An informational RFC from IBM describing the thinking behind Network/440, an experimental computer networking project at IBM Research in Yorktown Heights. The project aimed to understand networking, find design problems and implement solutions.

plainLanguage.summary: This informational RFC describes IBM's Network/440 design ideas. It separates network job management from the component that moves messages and outlines how the design handles message blocks and errors.

questions: what did ibm research learn from its network project
what is the logical network machine
how did network/440 handle flow control
what did the network controller do
subtitle: IBM's informational description of the Network/440 protocol concept.

tldr.problem: A network protocol must coordinate message exchange, jobs, errors and resource limits across connected systems.
tldr.mechanism: Network/440 separates job-level work managed by a Network Controller from message handling and switching by an Express Exchange.
tldr.outcome: The RFC shares IBM's design concepts and experience from an experimental network; it is informational rather than a formal ARPANET protocol specification.

sections.title: The Network/440 Project
sections.content:
Network/440 was an experimental computer networking project at IBM Research. Its goals were to understand networking, identify design problems and implement solutions. The RFC presents both project experience and broader protocol ideas.

A central idea is a logical network machine: treating connected systems as parts of one large multiprocessor system, without tying the protocol to a particular physical network layout.
sections.plainLanguage: IBM used Network/440 to study network design and test solutions. Its design treated connected computers as parts of one logical system, even when their physical arrangement differed.

sections.title: Network Controller and Express Exchange
sections.content:
The Network Controller (NC) manages network jobs and the steps they contain. The Express Exchange (EE) handles communication and store-and-forward message delivery, allowing ordinary messages to move without intervention by the NC.

The RFC describes these functions as usable in different physical configurations. In a distributed network, an EE could forward messages to the next station; the NC would act when job-level control was needed.
sections.plainLanguage: The NC manages network jobs. The EE moves messages between stations, including messages that do not need a job-level decision.

sections.title: Blocks, Messages and Recovery
sections.content:
A transmission block is a physical unit containing a header and text. A logical message can contain several blocks. Header fields identify destinations, jobs and message blocks; flags mark the first and last blocks, while a logical message identifier helps reassemble blocks that travel among other traffic.

The protocol describes acknowledgements, retransmission, pauses and resumes. The EE and NC cooperate to manage errors, clear affected messages and restart work when a system becomes available again.
sections.plainLanguage: Messages can be split into labeled blocks and reassembled at their destination. The design includes ways to acknowledge, retry, pause and resume message traffic.
